title: Michael Jordan Turned $180 Million Into $3 Billion

beats.say: You know Michael Jordan for shoes, but he reportedly turned about one hundred eighty million dollars into three billion.
beats.visual: an empty basketball arena at night with a single spotlight on center court, no people

beats.say: In twenty ten, he bought the majority of a struggling team, then called the Charlotte Bobcats.
beats.visual: a lone basketball resting under a hoop in a dark gym, hard side light, no people

beats.say: The team lost a lot. In his years as owner, it made the playoffs only twice.
beats.visual: rows of empty blue stadium seats in dim light, wide shot, no people

beats.say: Most fans remember the losing, not the math.
beats.visual: a scoreboard dark and unplugged hanging in an empty arena, no text

beats.say: But the team's value was not about the scoreboard.
beats.visual: a glass trophy case with one empty shelf in a quiet hallway, no people

beats.say: There are only thirty of these teams, and the whole league's value kept rising.
beats.visual: thirty identical white chairs in a row on a dark stage, wide shot, no people

beats.say: In twenty twenty three, he agreed to sell the majority at about a three billion dollar valuation.
beats.visual: a gold key handed across a polished table in a boardroom, hands only, dramatic light

beats.say: He kept a minority stake, so he still owns a small piece.
beats.visual: a single gold coin resting on a dark wooden floor beside a basketball, close-up

beats.say: Here is the part nobody tells you. A bad season is not the same as a bad asset.
beats.visual: a stormy sky clearing above a quiet city skyline at golden hour, no people

beats.say: Scarce things in growing markets can gain value even while the results look ugly.
beats.visual: a tall stack of gold coins rising into a dark sky, dramatic low angle

beats.say: The honest catch: team values are not cash, owners can cover losses, and almost nobody can buy a team.
beats.visual: a stormy sea with waves rising under a heavy sky and a lighthouse in the distance

beats.say: So the lesson is not buy a team. It is ask what you own, and whether it is scarce.
beats.visual: a hand holding a single brass key up to the light, extreme close-up, no face

beats.say: Follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: an empty highway stretching toward a glowing sunrise horizon, wide shot

description: Michael Jordan reportedly paid about 180 million dollars for the Charlotte team in 2010 and agreed to sell his majority stake in 2023 at about a 3 billion dollar valuation. What owning a scarce asset did, and the honest catch.
first_comment: Would you rather earn the fee or own the team? Educational only, not financial advice.

facts.claim: 2010: Jordan bought the majority of the Charlotte Bobcats (later renamed Hornets); Front Office Sports reports about $180M, Forbes valued the team at about $280M
facts.basis: Front Office Sports; Forbes via Fox Business

facts.claim: 2023: agreed to sell majority stake to Gabe Plotkin and Rick Schnall at about a $3B valuation; Jordan kept a minority stake
The team made the playoffs rarely under Jordan (2014 and 2016)
Catch: team valuations are not cash; he also covered losses; few buyers can own a team

caption: Michael Jordan reportedly paid about $180M for a majority of the Charlotte team in 2010. The 2023 sale valued it near $3B. Ownership of a scarce asset, and the catch. Educational content, not financial advice.
